clue.text: Spot a record number of balls

parts.note: a record is a disc
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end

explanation.surface: Someone notices a record-breaking tally of deliveries in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' reads as a noun but is the verb. An OVER is cricket's set of six balls bowled in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to notice or find it, a synonym.

clue.text: Blue Boy turned up without practice

indicators.note: without means outside, so the reversed boy goes round the practice
turned up in a down clue means the boy is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a lad is a boy
an ism is a practice or doctrine

explanation.surface: Gainsborough's famous young sitter, out of training, arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue Boy' suggests Gainsborough's painting, but 'Blue' alone is the definition; 'turned up' reverses the boy (upwards in a down clue) and 'without' wraps it round the practice.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means feeling gloomy or depressed, a synonym.

clue.text: In Cornwall, I save tins for recycling

indicators.note: recycling suggests the tins are reprocessed, so their letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: A Cornish resident keeps old cans to be recycled.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the place's location: a seaside town in Cornwall, England's south-western county.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a resort town on the north coast of the Cornish peninsula, so a place found there.

clue.text: Dark blue looks neat on a Scotsman

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so an ox
taken as written
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: Navy suits a man from Scotland well.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford's sporting colour is dark blue, so its members are Dark Blues; 'neat' is not tidy but cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford University's colour is dark blue, so one of its members is a Dark Blue.

clue.text: From the damage incurred almost crack up

parts.note: ex means from, as in ex works

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the damage is dropped

parts.note: the toll is the damage or cost incurred

explanation.surface: Someone nearly breaks down from the harm suffered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crack up' looks like breaking down, but means praise highly; 'almost' cuts TOLL to TOL.
explanation.definitionFit: To crack something up is to praise it enthusiastically, a synonym.

clue.text: Reckless plan involving assistant

indicators.note: involving means the plan wraps round the assistant, holding it inside

parts.note: a map is a plan of an area
ADC is the abbreviation for aide-de-camp, an officer's assistant

explanation.surface: A rash scheme that drags in a helper.
explanation.definitionFit: A madcap person or idea is wildly impulsive, a synonym of reckless.

clue.text: Warned of broken treadle

indicators.note: broken means the treadle is smashed and its letters put back in another order

explanation.surface: Someone was told that a foot pedal had snapped.
explanation.definitionFit: To be alerted is to be given warning of danger, a synonym.

clue.text: Completely free

explanation.surface: Entirely at liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'clear through' it means wholly, and to be clear of debt or blame is to be free of it.

clue.text: What goes wrong in French country walks

indicators.note: in places the jumbled word inside the French word

parts.note: pays is French for country

indicators.note: goes wrong means the letters of the word what go astray into a new order

explanation.surface: Whatever goes awry on rambles through the French countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes wrong' scrambles the word what into THWA, and 'in' sets it inside the French word, between its second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Paths for walking along are tracks or footways.

clue.text: Begged — the Scarlet Pimpernel used to

explanation.surface: A plea, then a nod to the elusive fictional hero.
explanation.walkthrough: In Baroness Orczy's novel the Pimpernel is hunted everywhere: 'They seek him here, they seek him there'. So he was looked for, and the clue completes 'used to (be ...)'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the past tense of beseech, implored; and with 'be' it says the elusive hero was always being hunted.

clue.text: Unusual fish spotted here, and animal

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters of the next three words are set in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A rare fish has been sighted in this place, along with some creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges the fifteen letters of FISH SPOTTED HERE; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The camel is nicknamed this for carrying travellers across sandy wastes, so the phrase is a figurative name for that beast.

clue.text: A series of books introducing high-rise housing for workers

indicators.note: introducing means the first pieces lead in front of the next one

parts.note: NT is the New Testament, a series of books of the Bible
a hill is a rise that stands high

explanation.surface: A set of volumes presents tower blocks built for labourers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-rise housing' looks like tower blocks, but HILL comes from 'high-rise' alone and the definition is cryptic: the workers are ants.
explanation.definitionFit: Worker ants live in the mound they build, so it is housing for those insects.

clue.text: Way out west, about 1000 dollars became too much

indicators.note: about says the other pieces go round the money
out means the letters of the way are knocked out of their order

parts.note: a route is a way
G stands for grand, slang for a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: Somewhere out in the Wild West, a thousand-dollar sum got out of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges ROUTE to OUTRE; W follows, and 'about' puts G inside to make OUT-G-REW.
explanation.definitionFit: To grow beyond something, like a child with old clothes, is to become too big for it.

clue.text: Plainchant heard in ecclesiastical circles

parts.note: plain means flat or level, even
a chant is a song

explanation.surface: Plainsong is sung in churchy company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plainchant' looks like one word for church music, but splits into Plain and chant; the definition is the rest, a service heard in church.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Anglican evening service of prayer, sung in churches and cathedrals.

clue.text: At home, this mathematical line would be excessive

indicators.note: would be says that adding the home word would make the excessive word, so we take it away

parts.note: inordinate means excessive
in means at home

explanation.surface: Indoors, such a graph line would be too much.
explanation.walkthrough: Put IN (at home) before the answer and you get the word for excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: On a graph it is the vertical coordinate of a point, measured along an axis.

clue.text: Little boy in bad condition

explanation.surface: A small lad is in poor health.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky is a pet form of Richard; in British slang a dicky heart or knee is a weak, unreliable one.
explanation.definitionFit: A diminutive of Richard names a young lad, and the informal adjective means shaky or unsound.

clue.text: Fellow holding the two of hearts, a card that's inferior

indicators.note: holding says the fellow contains the letter taken from hearts

parts.note: a chap is a fellow

indicators.note: the two of means the second letter of the word hearts

parts.note: a jack is a playing card

explanation.surface: A man clutching the deuce of hearts, a low-value card.
explanation.walkthrough: The playing-card picture misleads: 'the two of hearts' is its second letter, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap-jack goods are shoddy and of low quality, a synonym.

clue.text: Steal a painting

explanation.surface: Make off with a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb it is a formal word for remove or purloin; as a noun, an abstract is a non-representational artwork.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstract is to take away, so to purloin; an abstract is a non-figurative artwork.

clue.text: Herb is a man's name

explanation.surface: A plant shares its name with a man.
explanation.definitionFit: An aromatic kitchen plant used in pesto, and also a given name for males.

clue.text: Fancy an older man

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or reworked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking a liking to a more mature gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as the verb 'be attracted to', but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a male given name, an example of a man.

clue.text: Customarily admitted, yet Freud analysed it

indicators.note: analysed suggests breaking the words up and examining them, so their letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Something habitually accepted, though the famous psychoanalyst picked it apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Customarily' looks like 'usually', but means 'at customs': goods let through without tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods allowed through Customs without paying tax are exempt from the levy.

clue.text: Loud reprimand — how terrible

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
an earful is a stern telling-off

explanation.surface: A noisy telling-off, and how awful it was.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearful can mean dreadful or very bad, as in a fearful mess.

clue.text: Free renegade imprisoned by soldiers

indicators.note: imprisoned by means the renegade is shut inside the soldiers

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers
a rat is a traitor or renegade

explanation.surface: A turncoat is released after being held by troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gratis costs nothing, so it is given without charge.

clue.text: Reducing the size of type, how one finally winds up

indicators.note: reducing the size of means each of the three words that follow is cut short by its final letter

explanation.surface: Shrinking a font size is how somebody ends up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reducing the size of' drops the last letter of type, how and one, leaving TYP, HO and ON; 'finally' points to those last letters going.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent tropical cyclone is a storm of whirling winds that whips up over the ocean.

clue.text: Stage fairies can be heard

indicators.note: can be heard means the word for fairies is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: fays is an old word for fairies

explanation.surface: Fairy folk on a theatre stage are audible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' looks like the theatre, but means a step in a process.
explanation.definitionFit: A phase is a step or period in a process, a synonym.

clue.text: One in claque gives tongue

explanation.surface: A member of a hired applause squad speaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: A claque is a group paid to applaud; a bell's clapper is called its tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired applauder strikes hands together, and the swinging striker inside a bell is its tongue.

clue.text: Animal essential to Bacchic or- : gies

indicators.note: essential to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A creature indispensable to drunken revels.
explanation.walkthrough: Bacchic means wild and drunken, after Bacchus, the god of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A corgi is a short-legged Welsh dog, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Really unimaginative man takes precedence

indicators.note: takes precedence means the man's name comes before the other piece

parts.note: Asa is a man's name, a king of Judah in the Bible
matter-of-fact means prosaic and unimaginative

explanation.surface: A truly dull fellow insists on going first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Really' sits as an adverb to 'unimaginative', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to mean in truth or actually, an idiom.

clue.text: Go round the finish with it

indicators.note: round says the attempt goes round the finish, enclosing it

parts.note: a go is a try or attempt
the finish is the end

explanation.surface: Take another lap past the finishing line, accompanied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with it' looks like a link phrase but is the definition, slang for fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being with it means fashionable and up to date.

clue.text: Objects to one old coin, takes after another

indicators.note: after says the next piece follows the second coin

parts.note: D was the abbreviation for an old British penny
the Roman numeral for one is I
S, a shilling, is another old British coin
to take to something is to like it

explanation.surface: Someone protests at being given a single antique coin, then grabs a second.
explanation.walkthrough: D (penny) and S (shilling) are pre-decimal British coins.
explanation.definitionFit: To object to something is to have an aversion to it, a synonym.
